lines.text: A small Buddhist kingdom high in the Himalayas, of cliffside monasteries and kings who measure happiness. This is the story of Bhutan.
In the eighth century, the teacher Padmasambhava, known as Guru Rinpoche, brought Buddhism to the valleys of Bhutan.
In the early thirteenth century, the first fortress-monastery rose at Thimphu, Tashichho Dzong, which now houses the throne room and the government.
In 1594 Ngawang Namgyal was born, the Zhabdrung, a lama who would come from Tibet and unite Bhutan.
In 1629 he built Simtokha Dzong near Thimphu, the oldest fortress-monastery still standing.
Nine years later came Punakha Dzong, at the meeting of two rivers.
In 1692 the Tiger's Nest monastery was built, clinging to a cliff high above the Paro valley.
In 1862 Ugyen Wangchuck was born. He would become Bhutan's first king.
His son Jigme Wangchuck, the second king, would keep the country closed and at peace.
In 1907 Ugyen was crowned, and the Wangchuck dynasty began, ruling to this day.
In 1929 the third king was born, Jigme Dorji Wangchuck, who would open Bhutan to the world.
By the middle of the century, the kingdom of Bhutan was finding its place among the nations.
In 1955 Thimphu became its capital, a quiet town in a high valley.
That same year the fourth king was born, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, who would bring both happiness and democracy to the heart of government.
In 1965 Tshering Tobgay was born, who would twice serve as prime minister.
In 1972 the young king set out a new idea: that a nation should be guided by Gross National Happiness, not wealth alone.
In 1980 his son was born, Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck, king since 2006.
In the early nineties a darker chapter: about a hundred thousand Nepali-speaking Bhutanese were forced out, to live for years in camps in Nepal.
In 2008 the king gave Bhutan a constitution, and the country became a democracy with an elected parliament.
And from 2023 a new city is planned in the south, Gelephu Mindfulness City, meant to bring jobs while keeping Bhutan's values.
From Guru Rinpoche to Gross National Happiness, Bhutan walks its own quiet path.
